title: Good time to come back to game dev?
author: Mekanofreak
selftext:
I have an honest question, and since ai is heavily involved, I felt this sub was a good place to have this discussion.

I spent years making small game project, lots of ideas on paper, but I never actually published anything. I made a few finished prototypes, some small game to learn, did a few non-gaming related coding project for work (I'm not in the tech industry at all, I work a trade job). 

As for my abilities, I dabbled in coding for a while as a hobby (learned unity script, then c#) , learned blender and even made some attempts at drawing and pixel art. The only thing I consider myself good at is writing (not in English mind you, it's not my first language.) I wrote many short stories and always received good reviews for them. 

The main reason I never made one of my *dream* games (I know this word is thrown around a lot, but bear with me I don't know how to describe it any other way) was always a lack of ressources (Day job not making enough to feed my family AND pay an artist for the art) , lack of time due to my day job or family, and sometime, my inability to actually code what I wanted in the game, and admittedly some scope creep and a bit of misplaced perfectionism. 

Now, I see what people use AI for, and to be frank, I used to be a bit anti AI, but am realising, like many other I believe, it's potential as a tool. I don't think it's a magic thing where you put a few words in and get your *perfect* project out, I've seen the "slop" games that are flooding the net. I know there's still a lot of work involved, but, as someone who's average at all aspect of making games exept maybe writing, do you think it's a good time to get back into it, learn to use AI to try and help my shortcoming and try to finally get some of those ideas out my head?

comments.author: tabaxi_gf
comments.body: Why not?  It’s very easy to learn how to make any software with ai. I would recommend starting small however. You can always build a prototype out.

comments.author: Manifesto-Engine
comments.body:
Yes. AI is reallyy useful for this now, especially if you already have ideas and some programming experience. Claude Opus 5.5 has been extremely capable for game development in my experience, but the biggest thing I’ve learned is not to just prompt “make my game.”

Start by building **editors and tools** for the parts you care about. Make an editor that establishes your art direction, another for creatures/items/worlds/levels, whatever your game needs. Then you’re giving the AI actual systems and constraints to build around instead of asking it to invent everything from scratch every time.

Keep the scope small at first, play what it makes constantly, and treat the AI like a very fast developer you still have to direct and review. You’ll absolutely still hit bugs, bad architecture, weird design decisions, and scope creep.

But for someone who has ideas sitting around because art, coding time, or implementation skill was the bottleneck? I think this is probably one of the best times to try again.

replies.author: Mekanofreak
replies.body:
I already started working out how to work with vscode and co-pilot a few days ago. Started messing with the AI to make just a simple prototype, and I'm impressed so far the ability to just ask the AI questions on how to set everything up also greatly helped. I haven't tried Claude code yet, I'm used to coding in either notepad++ and vscode for my unity projects back in the days, so that's why I'm using it, and a copilot Github pro subscription was only 10 bucks and it's plenty for my test so far. 

I'm, also learning comfyui on the side at the same time for some prototype artwork.

replies.author: liatris4405
replies.body:
This is just my personal opinion, but honestly, since I hardly ever write code by hand anymore, I think knowing the basics of tools like VS Code is enough. It helps to at least know where to click to view the code.

If you’re going to learn programming, I’d put more emphasis on software design: things like understanding why it’s a good idea to separate data from code from the start, or how the project’s folders are organized. AI can handle most of this, but knowing enough to work through those details with it at the beginning can significantly reduce development time.
